text: Ten lessons in, it's worth stepping back and seeing the whole shape of what actually got built, before looking ahead to what comes next.

The stack is small, and every piece earned its place. Northfield's August order exports sat in S3, in northfield-raw-zone under orders-raw. A Glue Crawler, northfield-orders-raw-crawler, scanned those files and registered them as a real table, orders_raw, in the Glue Data Catalog. And Athena ran ad hoc SQL straight against those files, no warehouse, no loading step, answering a real business question: Camp Kitchen leads on units sold, Tents and Shelters leads on revenue.

Along the way, two real complications showed up, the kind every production data project eventually hits. Lesson 5 found the crawler had inferred order_date as a plain string instead of a date, and showed two ways to fix it. Lesson 8 showed what a flat, unpartitioned file layout actually costs once data grows, and how to retrofit partitioning onto it.

The real skill underneath all of this wasn't the SQL. It was turning a vague ask into something specific in Lesson 1, building only as much infrastructure as that specific question actually needed in Lesson 2, and presenting the result honestly, nuance and caveats included, in Lesson 9. That pattern applies to every data project, not just this one.

Here's what changes next. The Intermediate project introduces a second stakeholder who needs this kind of answer not once, but every month — a repeatable dataset, not a one-time snapshot. That single shift, from ad hoc to recurring, is what justifies building a Glue ETL job to automatically clean and reshape the data into a curated zone, partitioned from the start this time, and the beginning of real scheduling so nobody has to manually re-run a crawler every month.

Further out, the existing Advanced capstone picks up from there, adding Redshift and Step Functions and the production practices that turn this into a genuinely job-ready project. But that's a different project, for a different, bigger requirement. This one is done — and it answered a real question, the right-sized way.
